BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Following this systems exit early Sunday, upper-level ridging will bring a brief dry period before the next system begins to move in.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mild and dry Wednesday through early Friday. Near record high temperatures.
- Chance of precipitation returns Friday night, with additional rain and mountain snow, along with cooler temperatures, through the weekend into next week.
- Windy this week, increasing and becoming very gusty Friday through Sunday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Clouds continue to stream across the area as temperatures warm in building heights aloft. The cold pool in the lower treasure valley is warming up on track with the forecast, though a little under numerical consensus. As warm temps continue through thursday the cold pool will continue to degrade. Temperatures will warm up to about 10-20 degrees above normal, with afternoon highs in the lower valleys approaching 70 degrees in many areas. Winds each day remain somewhat gusty out of the SE, enhancing valley warming. Gusts 15 to 20 mph are possible in open areas and SE-NW funnels/gaps. Temperatures for many areas will approach daily records, and skies remain partly cloudy with period of clearing through the short term.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: A deep cut off low pressure system will be moving onshore and east of the area through the weekend. Strong south/southwesterly flow aloft will increase during the day Friday as the system moves into the Pacific NW, with wind gusts 35-50 mph across the open terrain of southeast Oregon and far southwest Idaho, and 20-40 mph elsewhere. High temperatures on Friday will remain near record highs, warmest across the lower valleys of southwest Idaho, as the system moves in. The trough will weaken and become more of an open wave Friday into Saturday as it moves over the area, with a cold front moving west-to- east as well. Precipitation chances will rise to 50-90% Friday night through Saturday morning, highest across the mountains. Precipitation chances will gradually taper off through the day Saturday. Snow levels will begin the event 7-8 kft MSL and lower to 6 kft MSL by the end of the event. Winds will remain gusty on Saturday, but not as strong as Friday. Highs Saturday will cool 5-10 degrees from Friday.

Following this systems exit early Sunday, upper-level ridging will bring a brief dry period before the next system begins to move in. Another deep cutoff low moving inland from the Gulf of Alaska will be the weather maker early next week, bringing a 40-60% chance of precipitation to the area. Previous forecast models had this system moving in Sunday but recent trends and agreement have it now on Monday and Tuesday. Winds will weaken but continue to be breezy as the trough moves in. Temperatures will remain similar on Sunday, then cool several more degrees on Monday as colder air arrives with the trough. Snow levels are also forecast to lower to 4-6 kft MSL by Tuesday. Precipitation chances trend lower on Tuesday, but troughing overhead will keep conditions unsettled with temperatures cooling a few more degrees.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: Fall-like weather will likely return by Saturday or Sunday, with temperatures nearing seasonal normals for the first time in a while. Ensemble guidance is in good agreement of cooler temperatures sticking around through the rest of the forecast period.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above normal temperatures and dry conditions will likely prevail through Friday.
- Increasing chances for light mountain rain/snow and rain showers for portions of the plains by this weekend.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Slightly cooler temperatures are expected on Wednesday due to weak cold air advection aloft as eastern Colorado will be situated on the eastern edge of the well-advertized upper level ridge. However, it will still be warm, with highs in the low-to-mid 60s across the plains. Similar to the past few days, quiet weather will prevail with mostly clear skies.

On Thursday and Friday, the axis of the upper level ridge will shift east, allowing slightly warmer temperatures to return to the region. However, ensemble guidance has trended cooler these past few runs, so we don't have as good of a chance to hit 70 F in the plains. This is reflected in DESI probabilities dropping to 20-25% chance of temperatures meeting or exceeding 70 F. Regardless, we will stay dry across the region.

Guidance continues to hone in on a system this weekend bringing mountain rain/snow showers and possibly precipitation to portions of the plains. However, there are still many uncertainties with the track and evolution of this system that will impact how much mountain snow we will get and how widespread rain across the plains could be. Recent runs of the GEFS and ECMWF ensemble have trended towards a stronger shortwave trekking across Colorado, with some solutions resolving a closed low near southeast Colorado. However, models diverge with the track of the low pressure after that, with some tracks being too far south or east for our region to see the bulk of the expected precipitation. As of now, ensemble guidance is in agreement of light snow accumulations for the high country (mainly above 8000-8500 ft) Saturday through Sunday, and increasing chances for rain showers for our eastern plains on Sunday. It is still too soon to tell if the rest of the plains, including the Denver metro would see measurable precipitation from this system.

Fall-like weather will likely return by Saturday or Sunday, with temperatures nearing seasonal normals for the first time in a while. Ensemble guidance is in good agreement of cooler temperatures sticking around through the rest of the forecast period. There is a good signal that active weather will return by mid-week next week with multiple systems providing precipitation chances for the forecast area.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Tuesday...The flow aloft backs to south southwesterly in advance of the next approaching shortwave trough aloft.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Windy conditions are expected today alongside elevated fire weather concerns.
- Above average temperatures and dry conditions are expected to continue into and through the end of the week with our first chance of even meager precipitation expected on Saturday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Conditions remain benign in the short term forecast period as we see temperatures remain around 10 to 15 degrees above normal with minimal impacts expected. The most noteworthy feature of the forecast period is occurring today as a modest jet is seen over the area in relation to a dry trough moving across. Some breezy winds have been noted, the strongest of which across the I-25 corridor up through the Bordeaux area, but sensors utilized in the region are not reporting so it's hard to say to what extent the strongest conditions are, but a few gusts nearing 60 mph can't be ruled out in this corridor. The jet should continue to bring enhanced conditions through the evening hours before weakening thereafter. Otherwise temperatures remain on the warm side today with widespread highs in the 50's west of the Laramie Range, and 60's to near 70 to the east.

Into Wednesday temperatures will cool down slightly due to the system that just passed through the region, but don't expect a dramatic drop in highs. Widespread temperatures stay in the mid 50's to mid 60's as ridging begins to move back in and resume control of the region. We'll continue our dry and uneventful spell under this feature, with temperatures then warming a couple of degrees on Thursday.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Friday...The high amplitude ridge axis aloft moves from western Wyoming to western Nebraska by evening, with subsidence and dry air continuing the dry and mild trends. 700 mb temperatures near 5 Celsius will yield high temperatures from the mid 50s to mid 60s.

Saturday...The flow aloft turns southerly with falling heights as the next trough aloft approaches from the Great Basin states. Looks like adequate low and mid level moisture to produce scattered dynamic and orographic showers across our Snowy and Sierra Madre Ranges, with dry conditions elsewhere. Cooler temperatures with more opaque cloud cover overhead.
Sunday...The trough aloft opens up and moves into the Texas Panhandle by late in the day, with only some residual cloud cover, and no precipitation left over in our forecast area.
Monday...Another transitory ridge aloft moves overhead, keeping our weather dry and mild, with 700 mb temperatures trends suggesting slightly warmer surface temperatures.

Tuesday...The flow aloft backs to south southwesterly in advance of the next approaching shortwave trough aloft. Looks like enough low and mid level moisture for scattered rain and snow showers over much of Carbon County, including the Sierra Madre Range, with dry conditions elsewhere. Temperatures slightly cooler with additional cloud cover compared to Monday.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Early next week, models are hinting at another shortwave moving through the region bringing another round of precipitation and colder temperatures.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions and above normal temperatures will continue through the work week.
- The pattern is looking more active this weekend into next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: High pressure will persist through the week, bringing warm and dry conditions. Temperatures are expected to run 5-10 degrees above normal through at least Friday.

Models are coming into better agreement on a long-wave trough bringing several low pressure systems across the Western CONUS this weekend into next week. The first shortwave arrives Saturday with the potential for colder temperatures along with valley rain and mountain snow. In general the snow levels appear to range from 7-9 kft, which is lower than previous storms.

Early next week, models are hinting at another shortwave moving through the region bringing another round of precipitation and colder temperatures. Model agreement remains poor this far out, so be sure to stay tuned to see how the forecast develops over the coming days.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: The wave will move on pretty quickly, with the area drying out again later Sunday into Monday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Mountain showers arrive Saturday-Sunday, with rain over the plains.
- After a brief lull through about Monday, models suggest more active weather mid-late next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: A dry front will push over the plains from the north this afternoon, bringing a northerly wind shift though the area will remain dry. Temps tonight will be cool, with 30s to low-40s out east and 20s to low-30s over the valleys. For Wednesday, another mild fall day is in store, with high temps in the 50s-60s across the region. The area will once again remain dry, with fairly light winds and mostly sunny skies.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Weather will remain dry the rest of this week, with temperatures warming a few degrees on Thursday. Upper ridge overhead will remain in place until Saturday, when a wave will pass through and bring some high based showers to the Continental Divide. Light snow accumulations are expected throughout Saturday Night, with rain showers spreading to the eastern plains Sunday morning.

The wave will move on pretty quickly, with the area drying out again later Sunday into Monday. Model solutions quickly diverge further in the future, though recent trends suggest another broad trough moving into our region by the middle of next week, bringing in a cooler and more active pattern for our area.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: This trough will be the first in what looks to be a fairly active pattern which will continue into late next week. Following a brief break in the weather Sunday into Monday, models have another trough moving into the area on Tuesday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry conditions with valley inversions persisting through Thursday before valley rain and mountain snow arrive this weekend that will help to mix out the inversions.
- Another storm early next week could bring cooler temperatures aloft and more widespread precipitation, but confidence is low on the timing and track.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: High pressure is building back into the area this evening following the weak trough that crossed Utah early this morning. The trough did bring somewhat improved mixing owing to cooler air aloft, although a shallow, elevated inversion layer still exists. With the return of high pressure, which will strengthen into Thursday, expect inversions to strengthen once again, producing some valley haze but otherwise benign weather.

Southerly flow will increase on Friday ahead of the next storm system. These winds may not be strong enough to mix out all valley inversions, but there will be a potential for improvement, especially west of I-15. The storm system itself is still progged to arrive on Saturday as a relatively fast-moving open-wave trough, bringing widespread valley rain and mountain snow to the forecast area. Models are coming into better agreement with this solution, with only around 28% of ensemble members holding on to a weaker trough and drier solution. The NBM now has greater than 0.2 inches of QPF over the mountains and I-15 corridor even at the 25th percentile, compared with yesterday where little to no measurable precipitation was indicated at the 25th percentile. At the 75th percentile, the NBM has many mountain areas exceeding 1 inch with valleys generally greater than 0.2 inches to upwards of 0.75 inches. Snow amounts in the 4-8 inch range is currently forecast for the mountains.

This trough will be the first in what looks to be a fairly active pattern which will continue into late next week. Following a brief break in the weather Sunday into Monday, models have another trough moving into the area on Tuesday. This looks to be a slightly cooler system which has the potential to bring snow to at least the higher valleys (around 5000-6000 feet).

2660.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Avalanche conditions are generally safe. Avoid isolated pockets of wind-drifted snow above treeline. Clear and warm days keep the prospect of wet, loose avalanches in the picture in the afternoon on southeast, south, and southwest slopes.

2747.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe for travel, holding too little snow to produce an avalanche. At high elevations, steer around firm, drifted snow below ridges or in deeper gullies.

2842.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has yet to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. Except on the steepest, highest-elevation, north-facing slopes, the mountains are snow-free. Avalanches will be unlikely until a deeper, layered snowpack builds. Once winter does arrive, even a small amount of snow with enough wind can create unstable avalanche conditions. If you're traveling in the mountains during or after a storm, be wary of steep, wind-loaded features at upper elevations and watch out for terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information as more snow accumulates
hazard_discussion: Due to a warm and dry fall season, the mountains in our forecast zones remain mostly dry, with little to no snow on the ground. As you're waiting for winter to arrive and the mountain snowpack to stack up, here are a few things to consider:
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

2755.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe from avalanches. On isolated slopes at higher elevations, you might encounter stiffer slabs over weak layers 1 to 2 feet deep on the north side of the compass. Look for stiffer snow surfaces or rounded drifts below ridges or in terrain depressions as features to avoid, especially in steep, consequential terrain.
